The National Assembly. Twenty-first session. Complete Proceedings. Monday, Jestha 2083. Meeting Number - 4. The National Assembly's meeting today commenced at 13:20 under the chairmanship of the Honorable Chairperson Mr. Narayan Prasad Dahal. (13:20) Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable members, the proceedings will now commence. I have allocated one minute each for honorable members to speak during the Zero Hour. First, Honorable Member Gita Devkota. Honorable Member Gita Devkota (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, I want to draw the serious attention of the government to the eviction of settlements in various districts, including Chitwan, in the name of removing squatters and those who have come from outside the country. In a democracy, it is the state's responsibility to provide proper alternatives, dignified housing, and rehabilitation without displacing citizens. Evicting settlements without ensuring proper alternatives, dignified housing, and rehabilitation leaves thousands of poor citizens insecure and victimized. On the other hand, the risk of floods, landslides, and inundation is increasing in various areas, including Chitwan, which have started in the past. Citizens living on riverbanks and in coastal areas are forced to live in fear. In such a sensitive situation, the government should not just issue directives. It is necessary to immediately and effectively engage in preparedness, safe relocation, embankment construction, rescue, and relief management. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Chandra Bahadur KC. (13:22) Honorable Member Chandra Bahadur KC (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, my first demand is the immediate resolution of the squatter issue without causing distress. I request the management of the market for coffee cultivation in Gulmi district and the budget as per the demand. This is a coffee industry inaugurated by King Birendra in 2042 BS. I request a budget of Rs. 24 crore for the road from Resunga Municipality Ward No. 3 to Siddhababa Temple in two Gulmis for this fiscal year. Thank you, Jai Nepal. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Jagat Timilsina. (13:23) Honorable Member Jagat Timilsina (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, a news report published in Online Khabar on Jestha 30, 2083, stated that 784 professors draw salaries from Tribhuvan University but teach in private institutions. It is mentioned that permission is taken by charging Rs. 2500 per person, citing the provisions of the Tribhuvan University Monitoring and Regulation, 2063. The news is objectionable that professors are being publicized in this manner when they are doing the teaching and examination work assigned by the university's educational institutions, whether campuses or departments, and working outside for the remaining tasks. (Time expired.) Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Meenasingh Rakhala. (13:24) Honorable Member Meenasingh Rakhala (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Chairperson, farmers are extremely distressed due to wild animals like wild boars and monkeys destroying their crops in various parts of the country, including Dailekh. Many have been forced to leave their land fallow as they cannot protect the crops they cultivated with a day's sweat. The crops are destroyed overnight. In Dailekh's Bhairavi Rural Municipality, citizens have lost their lives due to attacks by wild boars. The government is silent. Farmers are migrating. Does the government not listen to the farmers' pain? If farmers don't survive, agriculture won't survive. If agriculture doesn't survive, how will the country's self-reliant economy survive? Therefore, my demand is to immediately provide compensation to the affected farmers, arrange for safe farming, and expedite long-term solutions for wild animal control, and this should be addressed in the current budget. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Ranjit Karna. (13:25) Honorable Member Ranjit Karna (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, first of all, I want to salute the government's unprecedented dynamism. The flood of good governance has swept the country to such an extent that the opposition has to warn the public not to drown in it. Where is the national vision of the ruling and opposition parties working together to build the country? The government is busy proclaiming, 'I am the state.' I am amazed by one of the government's revolutionary decisions. The government's decision to ban trade unions in the name of reforming the bureaucracy is dictatorial. The government is disregarding the right to form associations and the right to labor guaranteed by Articles 17 and 30 of the Constitution. According to the Office of the Auditor General, capital expenditure in the first 10 months of the current fiscal year is only 27.51 percent. The problem lies in the expenditure system and implementation capacity. But the blame is placed on the unions. Democracy runs on dialogue and the constitution, not on the government's monopoly and arrogance. We are in constructive opposition. We will continue to show the mirror to the government when it deviates from the path. I hope this government will clean the mirror and... (Time expired.) Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri. (13:26) Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, a few days ago, the police arrested the CEO of Investment Mega Bank. The accusation is that the CEO should reveal whose liquidated residual asset it is. However, without considering the bank's accounts, prevailing laws, and standards, the CEO is being accused of providing loans from public savings and protecting the CEO by asking whose asset this residual asset was and who had priority. Such accusations and slander are intimidating CEOs and private sector individuals, preventing them from working. The government's actions in the name of good governance and quality service delivery are condemnable, and the government should pay attention to this. I reiterate that the days of ruling by intimidating people will soon end. Therefore, attention should be paid to this, and the prevailing laws should be respected. The police should also respect the law. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Rekha Kumari Jha. (13:28) Honorable Member Rekha Kumari Jha (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, the public is disappointed as the policies and programs are not as they expected. The public seeks change. The public seeks employment in their country. However, there is fear and apprehension among the public. For instance, poor Dalits without land ownership have been living in the municipalities of Madhesh Province, and now their sleep is disturbed, fearing that bulldozers might come to their homes. The public is wondering where the country is heading. I want to tell the Honorable Prime Minister that the public needs employment and development. Otherwise, the public is in distress, and you should respect their trust. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Roshi Mechhe. (13:29) Honorable Member Roshi Mechhe (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, today, through this house, I want to draw the government's serious attention to the deteriorating peace and security in the country. Incidents like murders, violence, theft, and robbery across the country, such as the two youths in Patan, the three-year-old child in Siraha, and the women murdered in Pokhara and Shivapuri, have created an atmosphere of fear among the general public. Furthermore, the alarming incidents of online fraud, foreign employment fraud, and cybercrime nationwide show a lack of sensitivity from the two-thirds government on serious issues like peace and security, which are fundamental and basic rights of citizens. Even though 27 days have passed since the Home Minister was embroiled in controversy and resigned, the Prime Minister, who is also holding the responsibility of the Home Ministry, seems to be more focused on populism and stunts than on the basic rights and problems of the people. Honorable Chairperson, therefore, I urge the government to immediately improve the peace and security situation, take effective steps to control crime, and create an environment where the public feels that the government is with them. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Samjhana Devkota. (13:30) Honorable Member Samjhana Devkota (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, the report of the Gauri Bahadur Commission, formed unilaterally by the government regarding the incident of Bhadra 23 and 24, which always pains us, was controversial even before its report was released. Concurrently, the National Human Rights Commission formed an investigation committee, and it has been two months since the investigation committee, led by one of its own officials, submitted its report to the commission. However, the commission itself has not yet investigated the report of this investigation committee. This indicates a tendency to keep the commission's report silent and misleading, and the public's trust and faith in constitutional bodies are diminishing. Therefore, I urge the government to immediately make the Human Rights Commission's report public, and as is being demanded even from the streets, the government should immediately... (Time expired.) Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Somnath Poudel. (13:31) Honorable Member Somnath Poudel (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, our country purchases petroleum products from the Indian Oil Corporation. We are all aware of this. The government is selling diesel at Rs. 67 per liter, petrol at Rs. 48 per liter, and LPG gas at Rs. 555 per cylinder more than in the Indian market. Despite selling at such high prices, the government claims that the Oil Corporation is incurring losses. I am unsure if I don't know how to calculate this or if the government doesn't know. I would like to request the Honorable Chairperson to arrange for a reliable, trustworthy, and good chartered accountant to present the accounts. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable members, the Zero Hour concludes here. Honorable members, regarding the words used by Honorable Member Chand Bahadur K.C. in the meeting of the Assembly held on Jestha 31, 2083, in response to the reference made by Honorable Member Padam Bahadur Pariyar as per the rules, the Secretariat studied it and found that the Honorable Member used words like 'laato' (dumb) and 'andho' (blind), which are contrary to the provisions of Rule 291(d)(1) of the National Assembly Rules, 2075. Therefore, I instruct the Secretariat to remove these words from the Assembly records. Honorable members, a letter regarding the formation of the Council of Ministers has been received from the Office of the President. I will now inform you of the contents of the said letter. The Honorable President Ram Chandra Paudel, in accordance with the recommendation of the Honorable Prime Minister, has formed the Council of Ministers on Jestha 31, 2083, with the existing Council of Ministers formed on Chaitra 13, 2082, under the leadership of the Honorable Prime Minister Balendra Shah, by appointing, reshuffling, and assigning responsibilities as follows, in accordance with the Constitution of Nepal. The details are as follows: 1. Mr. Balen Shah, Prime Minister, Defense, Home Affairs, Science, Technology, and Innovation. 2. Dr. Swarnim Wagle, Minister of Finance. 3. Mr. Shishir Khanal, Minister of Foreign Affairs. 4. Mr. Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, Minister of Energy, Water Resources, and Irrigation. 5. Mr. Sunil Lamshal, Minister of Physical Infrastructure Development.

Honorable Members, the discussion will now commence on the proposal presented by the Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle, stating, "Let's discuss the principles and priorities for the upcoming fiscal year 2083/084 regarding the Appropriation Bill, excluding tax proposals."
Honorable Members, the names of the Honorable Members have been presented on a party basis to participate in the discussion on the said proposal. Now, I will provide time to the Honorable Members to participate in the discussion in order.
First, Honorable Member Narayan Dutt Mishra, time 15 minutes. Following this, Honorable Member Jhaku Prasad Subedi.
Honorable Mr. Narayan Dutt Mishra (Nepali Congress):- Respected Chairperson,
(13:38 hrs)
Looking at the principles and priorities of the presented Appropriation Bill, 2083, some things come to mind. The country is currently in various kinds of difficult situations. When the country is going through a difficult economic situation, it is natural for the public to expect hope, trust, and clear direction from the government. The presented principles and priorities show the government's great desire and ambition, but the basis for implementation is not strong. The meaning of principle is to be based on established facts. The question arises: are all five guiding principles of the Appropriation Bill, 2083, based on facts?
The question can be raised. These principles are: 1) Dividend of Good Governance, 2) Restructuring of the Economy, 3) Integrated Infrastructure for Connectivity, 4) Universal Social Upliftment and Expansion of the Middle Class, and 5) Strengthening Renewable Energy. As we move forward, the meaning of principle does not seem clear everywhere.
Respected Chairperson, this government was formed with the strong support of the youth, who are internationally recognized as the Gen Z generation. I am concerned that the frustration of these youth might increase. The names of Australia, America, Canada, Britain, European countries, and Japan are frequently heard from the mouths of young and educated manpower. There are no clear priorities to stop this in the country. Farmers, who are considered the backbone of this country, have the same problems all the time. The scarcity of fertilizer always troubles them. Quality seeds and irrigation are their traditional problems, while not getting even the minimum price in the market is a constant issue. The government does set a minimum price sooner or later, but it is limited to paper and a few influential people. The tendency to embezzle even subsidies in the name of farmers through collusion between some brokers and employees continues.
The morale and confidence of industrialists and traders are wavering. The government's priority in the operation of rural industries always remains limited to paper, books, and booklets. In such a situation, the priorities brought by the government should have focused on production, employment, and economic reform. However, looking at the documents, it seems to be merely declarative. Nevertheless, rather than making many comments now, it can only be judged by looking at the budget management and its implementation. There are many problems. The principles and priorities seem to have tried to light a lamp to find solutions. But it's like an old wick, not even a lantern, but like a kerosene lamp. If you try to walk on the path holding a kerosene lamp, if you try to look in one direction, it seems like a shadow falls in another direction. Every year, a small amount of capital budget is allocated, but it cannot be spent, and the budget is transferred from one place to another.
Development projects remain incomplete, and are kept pending. A strange practice also causes difficulties in the construction of projects in the country. That is, the situation where they seem to sleep for eight months of the year, work for two months, and rush the work in the last two months makes it impossible to achieve quality work. Bills are prepared, but the government has neither new machinery nor any concrete action plan to solve this problem.
I really want to talk about agriculture. Not just talk. It is difficult for Nepal's GDP to leap forward without agricultural development. Although the agricultural sector is said to be prioritized, it seems that one aspect has not been considered. Have measures to reduce the cost of production for farmers been considered or not? There is no provision for ensuring a suitable market for farmers, nor are there any concrete action plans for achieving self-sufficiency in agriculture. Similarly, the direction of modern agricultural transformation has not come clearly. No concrete plans have come for storage and processing either. There is also a lack of planning on which sector's production should be specially emphasized to substitute imports. I say agriculture, agriculture, agriculture. The government should focus on multi-dimensional agriculture. Empower the ward offices, make them capable.
No clear vision for providing employment has been presented to make the minds of the youth stay in the country. It is necessary to have a clear understanding and strategy from the government on which sector can create how much employment and which sector can be made a center of attraction for employment, in terms of skills, development, and entrepreneurship. Today's generation is waiting with many expectations from this government. If their expectations turn into neglect, today's generation is not in a state to mourn much in their dreams. They are looking for results and opportunities. If the Gen Z group, already divided into various factions and dissatisfied with the government, cannot be reassured by concrete plans, it cannot be said that the country will not fall into a quagmire.
Respected Chairperson, to combat rising unemployment, it is essential to move forward as a partner in the economy by gaining the trust of the private sector. Employment can be created only by improving the investment environment, simplifying administrative hassles, creating an environment for quick and efficient business operations, and giving confidence to industries and businesses. It is necessary for the government to move forward with a partnership perspective rather than a suspicious one towards the private sector.
Democratic republic is also the decentralization of power and resources. I feel that we have not been able to get rid of a centralized perspective. Our administrative mentality wants to see decentralization only up to ourselves. Therefore, considering the laws and their enforcement, and keeping federalism in mind, by distributing resources and authority according to the law, the country can only move forward by strengthening the governments at all three levels.
Another important point is that there is no possibility of development without good governance. No budget can be successful without controlling corruption, making the public sector fully transparent, and having a results-oriented administration. It is urged that the public should also feel the benefits of the taxes they pay. The success of the budget should be sought only by creating a production-oriented economy, truly prioritizing agriculture and industry, creating employment for youth within the country, distributing resources and authority according to the spirit of federalism, and implementing good governance in practice.
Respected Chairperson, in conclusion, as a member of the National Assembly and also of the Nepali Congress, I request the government. To create a production-oriented economy, to truly prioritize agriculture and industry, and to create opportunities for the youth to stay in Nepal. Furthermore, to distribute resources and power in accordance with the spirit of federalism, and to implement good governance in practice rather than just as a topic of speech, I humbly request the government. We want to assure you that with a positive mindset, playing the role of the opposition, we will support the work that is and will be done in the interest of the country and the people, and we will hold you accountable for your shortcomings. A strong opposition in a democracy is never an enemy of the government; it is a director of reform. There are many things I want to say within this bulletin. However, today I feel like saying one thing. Please do not be angry if I go a bit outside the scope of the program.
Respected Chairperson, the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill, 2083, have been prepared with much effort. If the budget management and implementation are done in the same way, we will be extremely happy. Once upon a time, Garuda, the vehicle of Lord Vishnu, went to Lord Shiva with a message from Lord Vishnu. As he was going to Lord Vishnu with the message, as soon as he bowed and greeted Lord Vishnu, the snake around his neck hissed and seemed to want to bite Garuda. Then Garuda said, "I know your power, O King of Serpents. You are roaring because you are around Shankar's neck." I do not want to go into that line because there is a parliament now, and sometimes there can be parliamentary or unparliamentary words, which I fear. Therefore, I will say the fourth line. "Sthanam pradhānam na balam pradhānam." That is, I say, "O King of Serpents, I know your power very well. You are roaring because you are around Shankar's neck." Place is important, not strength. I will not say the middle line now, as it would be incomplete. In a similar way, Garuda said, "O King of Serpents, if you were outside, you would have seen only my shadow flying above and would have quickly looked for a hole to escape into. Now, because you are around Shiva's neck, you are trying to show your influence a little. But look, many Garudas are flying in the sky. As soon as you come out of Shiva's neck, I have seen some ministers' PAs in such a situation. I don't want to say much to the ministers themselves, but please be mindful and careful. If you think you are surrounding the government now, then doing arbitrary work, today one thing, tomorrow opposition to that work, the day after tomorrow another thing, opposition to that work, the day after that another thing.

One by one, one after another, the government that is moving forward in a way that will mess up the country. I say that it will definitely come down to earth one day. Therefore, I am not able to complete the time, saying that the flock of eagles is flying, so please watch. Thank you. Jai Nepal.

Honorable Mr. Jhak Prasad Subedi (Nepal Communist Party): Honorable Chairperson

(13:52)
Sir, regarding the principles and priorities presented by the Honorable Minister for the fiscal year 2083/084, I want to raise some serious questions from the perspective of Nepal's leftist, people-oriented, and transformative political stream, especially the Nepali Communist Party. This principle and priority is not just the principle and priority of the government, it is not just a debate of priorities. It is a debate about the character of the state, the direction of development, and the hopes of the people. Looking at the principles and priorities of the budget, one thing is clearly visible: the government has not been able to free itself from the influence of the thinking of brokers, capitalists, and import-oriented economics. The thinking that prioritizes consumption over production, market over labor, import over self-reliance, and the private sector over social justice is clearly visible in this document.

It talks about a production-oriented economy, the previous honorable member also raised it, but there is nothing concrete as a basis for it. The government talks about agriculture, industry, and production. But the question is, why is the issue of land reform not mentioned here? Where is the guarantee of production for the farmers? Is the democratic restructuring of cooperatives not prioritized? The policy to protect local production is not seen here.

We are still dependent on imports for rice, vegetables, medicines, fertilizers, petroleum, and even common consumer goods. There are five points of principle here. Principles are mentioned from 9 to 19. Priorities are set from 20 to 40. But even that does not seem to be in a rhythm. The country's youth power is migrating abroad, but there is no revolutionary program in the budget priorities to connect the youth returning from foreign employment. The issue of social justice was necessary, but in the principles and priorities, the middle class and market orientation have come.

Sir, the constitution envisions a state oriented towards socialism, but there is no clear roadmap for socialism in the presented principles and priorities. Education and health are being pushed towards privatization rather than being the responsibility of the state. The tendency to facilitate the private sector rather than improve the quality of public schools and government hospitals is strong. The government has faith in the private sector. Who can build a high bridge? Who can build a tunnel? Now, even the work of Budhi Gandaki will be given to whoever can get it done by the government.

Now the question arises: is the state trying to become merely a regulator and not a service provider? Our perspective is clear. Education, health, employment, and social security are citizens' rights, not commodities for trade. If the middle class is the government's priority, what about the basic class? Much discussion has been done here about the middle class. The allocation for increasing the size of the middle class to institutionalize the democratic republic has come in the principles and priorities of the appropriation bill, 2083. It is stated in the government's document that a basis will be built for social security for those who need state protection. Will those who have been displaced from their homes without alternative arrangements in the name of protecting public land, those who are made to run bulldozers and terrorize the landless and unorganized settlers, and those who have apologized in parliament to Dalits, not have anything placed in their priorities? The most vulnerable class is the one that needs state protection the most. Here, such a ridiculous issue has come up. I want to focus a little on the middle class, which constitutes 20 percent of the population. Because this document is also centered around the middle class. How will the poor class, which is more than 20 percent of the population, be expanded into the middle class? Is the government expanding the middle class by bringing the lower class up, or by bringing the rich class down? Where are the programs to expand the poor in Sudurpashchim hills, where poverty is 42 percent, into the middle class? The middle class sustains their lives based on their fixed income.

After the US and Israel started a war with Iran, there was a significant price increase in fuel. Due to its impact, inflation increased in every sector. It has been almost three months since the war started. The biggest impact has been on the middle and poor classes. Has the government provided any relief to the middle class? When people's income remains the same but inflation increases in every sector, what is the government doing while the middle class's back is being broken by inflation? When people's income remains the same and inflation increases day by day, will the middle class expand or will the number of the poor expand, government? Fuel became expensive. Fares for vehicles increased. Transportation fares increased. Prices of rice, lentils, oil, sugar, vegetables, gas, and medicines increased. The main reason for bringing the expansion of the middle class as a priority is only to make the urban middle class a vote bank. If the class that goes to the Gulf countries wearing slippers and returns with slippers is what the government calls the middle class, then while the US wages war with Iran for a few months, the middle class's income will decrease, and the middle class's journey towards poverty will begin. If the government is in favor of the middle class, then open subsidized shops across the country. The middle class and the poor class are facing great difficulties at this time. The government is completely unaware. But it keeps it in its priorities, the expansion of the middle class. Bring principles and priorities based on facts.

Honorable Chairperson, distrust in federalism and provincial structures. The government talks about the implementation of federalism, but the actual practice of fiscal federalism has become even weaker. In the government's principles and priorities, there is a tendency to centralize power in the center rather than transferring authority to the provinces and local levels. The control of the center is still strong in revenue sharing, conditional grants, and project selection. This questions the spirit of the constitution. Federalism is not just an administrative structure. It is a transformation. It is also the democratization of all structures. It is also the overall economic and social transformation of this state power. But the current government's budget thinking is centralized, bureaucratic, controlling, and anti-basic class.

The government is silent on youth migration and unemployment. Honorable Chairperson, today the villages of Nepal are emptying. Youth are forced to sell their labor abroad. Agricultural land is becoming fallow, but the budget priorities do not have a clear national plan to provide employment to the youth within the country. Words like startup, innovation, and digital economy are used, but they seem to be mainly urban-centric and for the elite class. They are not at all for the poor. There is no clear vision to connect rural youth with production, agriculture, processing, green industries, and the local economy. There is no concrete commitment against corruption and the broker economy. The biggest problem of the country's economy is not just a lack of resources. It is also the wrong distribution of resources and the influence of broker capital. The government's priorities seem weak on large contracts, intermediaries, policy capture, tax evasion, and inequality in access to banking.

As the state's resources remain concentrated in the hands of a limited class, despair is growing among the people. If economic policy is not in favor of the people, the slogan of development will remain confined to speeches only. There is a lack of a transformative perspective.

Honorable Chairperson, the principles and priorities of this budget are management-oriented, not transformative. It seeks to make some improvements to the existing structure but does not challenge structural inequalities. We need not just economic growth, but equitable economic growth. We need not just infrastructure, but economic policies that change the living standards of the people. We need not just private investment, but a development model based on labor, production, and national self-respect. Therefore, I urge the government to prioritize a production-oriented economy. Bring a clear program for land reform and agricultural revolution. Strengthen education and health as full public responsibilities. Implement fiscal federalism in practice. Launch a national campaign to create employment for youth within the country. Take strict action against broker capitalism, corruption, and policy capture. A people-oriented budget should be created in accordance with the socialist-oriented spirit of the constitution. From this, it becomes politically clear which class this government stands for. The federal democratic republic built by the labor, sweat, and sacrifice of the people should be in favor of the basic people, not under the control of the profit-seeking market. I urge the government to pay serious attention to this. Thank you.

Honorable Mr. Prem Prasad Dangal (Nepal Communist Party, UML): Honorable

(14:03)
Sir, I seek permission to present some statements, comments, and suggestions from my party regarding the principles and priorities of the appropriation bill, 2083/084, presented by the Honorable Finance Minister. There are some good things, which do not need to be discussed. Some suggestions, some of our perspectives. I seek permission to present some opinions among you to make this document even better.

In a parliamentary democracy, the appropriation bill is the main tool that gives the government the legal authority to spend funds from the state treasury. It is a global practice to present it to the parliament before the budget. Its main theoretical aspect is to set the fiscal direction before the budget, which outlines the definite direction and policy framework for the budget of the upcoming fiscal year. It prevents the government from spending arbitrarily and strengthens fiscal discipline and accountability. As a result, the government is compelled to be fully accountable to the parliament financially. Its other most important democratic aspect is to ensure transparency and parliamentary supremacy. This ensures that representatives are widely involved in policy debates before the finalization of the budget, strongly ensuring that the aspirations of the people and the actual needs of the citizens are included in the annual budget.

Honorable Chairperson, the document regarding the principles and priorities of the appropriation bill for the fiscal year 2083/084 seems more like a political speech than a concrete economic roadmap, presented without a real analysis and factual data of the country's current economic situation, estimated GDP, growth rate, inflation, revenue projections, and expenditure limits. The reality that when trying to cover all sectors by arranging the principle of efficient allocation of resources, nothing becomes a priority, is realized. This creates an imbalance between limited resources and overly ambitious commitments.

Despite new funds and grants being proposed, ignoring the current fiscal pressure and debt burden, their sustainable source and structural guarantee are not disclosed. Honorable Chairperson, by merely repeating slogans without a clear implementation roadmap, this document...

The main challenge of the implementation crisis has not been addressed, and it appears to only superficially touch upon the existing economic stagnation and structural ailments. The presented document seems to have sidelined fundamental pillars of democracy such as financial discipline, accountability, transparency, and parliamentary supremacy. This has raised serious questions about the current government's commitment to democratic values and principles.

Honorable Chairperson, this document has failed in addressing the existing challenges in the economic sector. Specifically, there is a cyclical recession where investable capital is accumulating in banks, but there is no demand in the market. The crisis in cooperatives and microfinance has paralyzed the grassroots economy, and there is no clear direction for a concrete immediate relief package to boost the current financial crisis. Furthermore, there is no concrete action plan prioritized to end the perennial Nepali problem of inefficient budget spending only in the month of Asar. This makes the foundation for making the capital expenditure system efficient and effective weak.

In the social sector, the country faces the biggest national crisis as thousands of youth and skilled manpower are leaving, putting the nation at risk of becoming an old age home. There is no concrete economic incentive package to retain youth in the country and bring back those who have gone abroad. Also, there is no guarantee anywhere in the priority list to control the market price of daily consumer goods and provide relief to the general public. The document also appears to be silent on the multidimensional crises that geopolitical upheavals and conflicts worldwide have created in Nepal. The tension in Russia, Ukraine, and the Middle East has jeopardized foreign employment, risking remittances and foreign exchange reserves, while the rise in fuel and food prices has created inflation in the country. The polarization of power blocs has challenged Nepal's non-aligned foreign policy and foreign aid. We see this happening not based on the students' studies but on the convenience of the teachers. This is happening all over the country. There are problems everywhere. To manage this better, the state budget, especially the state's plans, should be focused on education, health, and employment generation. This should be the principle and priority.

Indeed, there seems to be a lack of alignment between priorities and principles. This is why all our plans have been like this year after year, and this government, which we expected to be organized, has also turned out to be similar. The state's primary responsibility should have been to reduce structural inequality, exclusion, and imbalance of opportunity. Public services should have been expanded with equal access for underdeveloped regions, marginalized communities, and disadvantaged groups. Furthermore, the government had also spoken of seeking an apology to end the historical structural discrimination against oppressed communities. However, apart from one instance where the chairman of a ruling party spoke on the rostrum, we have not seen such apologies elsewhere. Therefore, when the government makes plans, we have to consider who truly needs priority and where. We moved forward with 40 proposals yesterday, advanced action plans, and have been moving forward with them. We are cooperating with the government. But we don't know if the government is listening or not, and the results will probably be known by looking at the budget on the 14th. The state of the country is like this. The government's emphasis should be on providing justice to the victims of conflict and bringing peace processes to a conclusion. The government's attention must also be drawn to these issues, and landless and squatters must be identified. Currently, they are being left in ruins. No specific plan is coming out. There are no priorities. What does this show? It shows that the government is not serious about these issues. Our suggestion is that landless and squatters need to be identified and arrangements should be made for land that can sustain their livelihoods, along with safe housing. With this suggestion, I will conclude my brief remarks here. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Goma Devi Timalsina, time 5 minutes. (15:57) After that, Honorable Member Bishnu Bahadur Bishwakarma. Honorable Ms. Goma Devi Timalsina (Nepal Communist Party): Honorable Chairperson, we are going to discuss the principles, allocations, and priorities of the Appropriation Committee 2083 today. Many have already discussed this. Where should I start, where should I start? I am completely confused. Our current government talks so much about good governance, saying it will bring good governance. Our elders did nothing. They should be thrown off the cliff, they say. Now, let's listen to the current government's ministers. We haven't even seen the ministers up close. We can't even meet other ministers. We haven't been able to meet the Prime Minister either, hoping he would come and speak here. What kind of members will come there? Please don't think I'm saying this with prejudice. Did we come here by clapping our slippers? We came here with our status. We didn't come by clapping our slippers. What status do we have? We have been agitating since 2007, through 2046, until the establishment of the republic. We have built our status politically. When someone has no political standing, and they say such things, I find it amusing, or I don't know what. If we were to laugh, we are not face-to-face, when would we laugh, with whom? And what would the member there, the MP, say? They show bravery by saying, 'Come, let's fight one-on-one.' Is this good governance? Honorable Chairperson, through you, I want to ask the ministers present here. Does it suit an MP to fight one-on-one? Try to make your MPs understand this properly. Try to explain to them not to misuse their position, and give us an answer. Is this what they call good governance? Good governance means everyone should get food, shelter, clothing, health, education, employment, and all other necessities. Everyone should get health and education. I heard a few days ago, mentioning the names of a few industries, that these industries will run. Gorakhali Rubber Industry, Bhukuti Paper Factory, Arghakhanchi Textile Factory, Janakpur Cigarette Factory, and many other industries were mentioned by our new ministers. But there is no sign of them now. And we will not send our youth abroad, we will bring everyone back within 100 days, we will give them employment, we will bring them here, they said. If you don't vote for the bell, you won't be able to come to Nepal, the sons told their mothers. Now the mothers have told their sons, 'Don't come, son. Our house has been demolished by the government.' Look at the irony. Is this good governance in our country? I want to ask this question. I have already mentioned that sick industries will run. Today, the judiciary has said to stop the bulldozer terror. It has said not to displace the public by using bulldozers. Yet, bulldozers are still operating. Bulldozers have not stopped anywhere. And we are talking about education. The children whose houses were demolished by those bulldozers cannot even study. The sick are not getting treatment. The elderly do not have a warm place to shelter. We take shelter from the rain in our homes. They have no place to shelter from the rain. (Time expired.) Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Bishnu Bahadur Bishwakarma, time 6 minutes. (16:02) After that, Honorable Member Renu Chand. Honorable Mr. Bishnu Bahadur Bishwakarma (Nepal Communist Party): Honorable Chairperson, I am about to present my views on the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill, 2083. First, I will present my views on the principles. a) It is stated that good governance will be established by making the state accountable and technology-friendly. Some issues like anarchy and lack of transparency have been brought under legal purview. However, the state of cultural and social transformation is dire. b) It is still common for people to lose their lives during marriage, Dalits to be killed in custody, and Dalits to be imprisoned for crimes committed by the wealthy. When will the government ensure good governance? Misgovernance prevails due to the lack of laws. Let social justice and good governance be strengthened. c) Integrated infrastructure will be built for reliability. The issue of climate change and disaster risk has been raised here. However, the most affected by this are the poor, Dalit, and landless communities. There is no proper management plan for this. Let a proper management program be formulated. d) Economic dynamism and social expansion with security assurance are mentioned. It seems that only the middle class has been focused on. What about the poor and those below the poverty line? Shouldn't the focus be on the disadvantaged groups? Or is it to bring the poor and disadvantaged groups into the middle class? Or to further develop the middle class? Clarity is needed. It is stated that participation will be ensured in economic opportunities, not just limited to inclusion. Why has our government forgotten proportionality? Where is the special provision? This is a provision stipulated in the constitution. Let the guarantee of rights, along with proportional inclusion, be ensured. Modernization of national industries based on traditional arts such as broom, bamboo, iron, clay, curd, and agriculture, including sisno, bhang, radi-paki, and potato, should be done. Only through this can employment be generated and a basis for an export-oriented economy be formed. e) It is stated that economic benefits will be derived from mature relationships with neighboring and friendly nations and INGOs. This has been taken as a guiding principle. Relying on this, will the policy of remaining dependent on an import-oriented economy lead to economic growth? On the other hand, there is no sign of border security. Without border security, hopes of economic progress are mere fantasies. Protecting the border and the people is the duty of the state. Where is the Nepal government's border protection? Let the Nepali Army be deployed on all the borders of the country. Perhaps because this is not happening, the country's borders are being encroached upon in broad daylight. Without this, neither the security of the country and its people nor self-reliance can be achieved. It is not good to try to run the country by exporting the nation's production, resources, and capabilities and relying on remittances. This will neither bring progress nor security to the country, nor make the country self-reliant. Now, towards priorities. It is mentioned that the development of the mining sector is part of modernizing regional resources for economic growth. I am confused about what 'mining development' means. Perhaps it could mean research, extraction, processing, utilization, and marketing of minerals. Isn't development about making something bigger from something small? Or making two, three, four, five from one? Can we make two or three from one mine? Perhaps not. Therefore, clarity is needed. While emphasis is placed on the use of underground water resources in the Terai-Madesh and lift irrigation in the hills, it is necessary to focus on canal systems and lift canal systems in the Terai-Madesh. This is because underground water resources go deep into the earth, and future consequences must be considered. It is written that multi-sectoral capital mobilization will be used for physical infrastructure and to promote a circular urban economy. Where has the idea of turning Kathmandu's waste into wealth gone? It is not a good thing that there is no fertilizer factory in an agricultural country. Let a policy be adopted to establish a fertilizer factory. For equality of opportunity, there is social investment. Although the education sector is government and private, the educational policy, type of education, curriculum, and textbooks should be the same. Children should be made competitive through the same type of education, not education for the rich and the poor. Inequality in education must be ended. Furthermore, impractical and commercialization must be stopped. It is a good thing that it is stated that the disadvantaged regions, marginalized communities, and those deprived of opportunities will be brought to high access. However, the government's proposed plans are not included in the priorities. They must be included and implemented practically by formulating action plans. What I understand is that this Appropriation Bill is not grounded in Nepal's reality. Wherever we go, whatever country we are in, it seems to be thought of as a digital age. Whether this applies to Nepal... (Time expired.) (16:03) Resumed: Honorable Chairperson Shri Narayan Prasad Dahal. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Renu Chand, time 5 minutes. (16:09) Honorable Ms. Renu Chand (Nepal Communist Party): Honorable Speaker, I am here to present my views on the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill, 2083. Building a socialist-oriented nation in accordance with the basic spirit of the constitution, through a production-oriented, inclusive, and self-reliant economy, must be the main theoretical basis. It has been made. It is written about establishing order. I would like to suggest that this should start by finding a solution to the absence and silence of the head of government in parliament. Otherwise, no one will believe your claims of establishing order. The excessive use of jargon makes it difficult for the general public to understand. Regarding its language, the Appropriation Bill prioritizes digitalization. How does it protect the freedom of expression of women? We are in a situation where we have to endure digital harassment just for expressing our views. Obscene comments, threats of rape, death threats. The indifference of the administration and the cyber bureau to this has made us women fed up and angry. This digital harassment has already taken the form of severe digital violence. The dignity of half the country's population...

Whether it is a priority or not. Now I want to mention some things about Sudurpashchim. It is a province with a unique geographical situation, bordering the important neighboring countries of India and China. We had raised this in the policy and program, but I want to mention it here by naming the plan to make it easier for the government. The Mahakali Corridor and Seti Lokmarg, Karnali Corridor need to be completed quickly. Our parliamentary committee has conducted an on-site visit of the Mahakali Corridor. The government can also take reference from its report today. After that, the matter of making the Mid-Hill Highway a double lane. Then, the government is urged to prioritize national policy reforms and financial assistance for the upgrading of provincial hospitals and strengthening of service delivery. I want to draw the government's attention to operate Shahid Dasharath Chand Health Sciences University at full capacity and immediately start teaching in all disciplines of medical education. The government's attention should also be drawn to the budget management of colleges and campuses affiliated with Tribhuvan University's constituent campuses but not receiving budget, such as Gokuleshwor Animal Science and Agriculture Campus, Pachauwa Campus, etc. Fapla Cricket Ground has been advanced as a dream project to establish Dhangadhi as a city of cricket. Its management should also be a priority for the government. These and many other matters have been registered by our press government in various bodies of the federal government. My suggestion to the government is to take them as reference points and include them in the upcoming budget. Similarly, I want to express my views by drawing the government's attention to the development and upgrading of quarantine laboratories at the border crossings of Sudurpashchim, namely Gachha Chowki, Trinagar, Khargola, Jhulaghat, and Darchela, and the implementation of an integrated customs system. The government is bowing down to the upper class, as it has written about the expansion of the middle class. I praise you for honestly declaring your class commitment. But you have failed to prioritize farmers, laborers, the oppressed, and the landless. The government cannot be partial. You have become incapable of seeing the suffering of poor landless women, and surprisingly, the youth agenda is not there. Why are the youth's agendas not included in this document? I want to ask the government. Anger has been generated by addressing the solution to the problem of landless people later and displacement first. How will this be resolved? Why is there no preparation? The government will also have to answer why it has started without preparation. What kind of development are you trying to achieve by terrorizing the private sector? How can it be done by demeaning and terrorizing private construction businesses and private sector entrepreneurs? This could not be understood. Similarly, what preparations have you made for Nepalis returning from the challenges seen in the Middle East? The tax on goods exceeding one hundred rupees was in the 1969 (2026 BS) regulations. How do you think it will be practical to implement it now? The open border directly connects Madhesh and Sudurpashchim. You have failed to understand the economic, social, and cultural aspects with India. They say divorce between plan and implementation. Always good on paper, challenges in implementation, I am worried that the destiny of this legislation will also be the same. Finally, I would like to conclude by suggesting that the government cannot be partial. Thank you. sections.name: Zero Hour
sections.summary_en: Several members raised concerns during Zero Hour. Gita Devkota highlighted issues of squatter eviction and disaster preparedness. Chandra Bahadur KC demanded resolution for squatters and budget for coffee farming and road construction in Gulmi. Jagat Timilsina raised concerns about professors drawing salaries from TU while teaching elsewhere. Meenasingh Rakhala spoke about crop destruction by wild animals and demanded compensation and solutions. Ranjit Karna criticized the government's approach to bureaucracy and trade unions, and highlighted low capital expenditure. Ram Kumari Jhankri condemned the arrest of a bank CEO and the government's intimidating tactics. Rekha Kumari Jha expressed public disappointment with policies and called for employment and development. Roshi Mechhe drew attention to the deteriorating peace and security situation, citing various crimes and fraud. Samjhana Devkota urged the government to make the Human Rights Commission's report public. Somnath Poudel questioned the pricing of petroleum products and the financial status of the Oil Corporation.
